newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala beef industry wallows in major slump.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala beef industry wallows in major slump.

text.p: Guatemalan cattle stocks have shrunk by one half since the 1980s and beef exports are also in a slump due to more profitable crops taking over ranching land, Agriculture Ministry officials said Tuesday.

"Since the 1980s the national cattle stock of four million head has seen a reduction of between 1.7 and two million. It has reduced 50 percent," Oscar Suchini, Deputy Agriculture Minister, told Reuters.

Suchini said cattle ranching has been displaced by crops, such as sugar, sesame and soybean, that are currently more profitable, and give a quicker return on investment. "Cattle exports have slowed down a lot," Suchini said.

In 1994, Guatemala exported $7.8 million worth of carcasses and boned fresh beef, $4.3 million in frozen beef, and $1.4 million of live cattle, to the United States, Central America and Puerto Rico, according to the National Statistics Institute.

In 1995, carcass exports disappeared altogether and fresh beef exports dropped 55 percent to $3.5 million. Frozen beef exports dropped 47 percent to $2.3 million. Live cattle exports dropped 93 percent to $0.1 million. Numbers for the first half of 1996 show a continued drop.

Suchini said the Mexican market, which used to be big for Guatemalan beef, was no longer financially viable due to 15 percent tariffs on live head, 20 percent for fresh meat and 25 percent for frozen meat.
Guatemala is seeking lower tariffs for beef exports to Mexico in ongoing trade negotiations with its northern neighbour, he said.
Meanwhile, the government is supporting a beef industry recovery effort focused on improving the quality of Guatemalan beef, according to the deputy minister.

Suchini said dairy and beef producers, meat packers, and livestock truckers have met to explore strategies including using special cattle transport trucks, improving health standards for herds and sanitary quality in slaughter houses and packing plants.
Edgar Sandoval, a cattleman who is president of the Registered Cattle Breeders Association, said the depressed beef industry has forced him to branch out into cut flower and coffee production.
Sandoval said 15-20 years ago, 60 percent of Guatemalan beef was exported and 40 percent consumed locally. Now, he said, about 80 percent is consumption and 20 percent exported.

There are four packing houses, all of them working at 10 percent of capacity, and which pay between $0.24 and $0.44 per pound for fattened steers, according to Sandoval. He said packers import some cheap beef from Nicaragua and Honduras, where prices are even lower.
Sandoval said high prices of grain mean few feed lots. Some 98 percent of cattle in Guatemala is grass fed, he said.
